analysis.one_liner: Adds a 10 percent tax on individual income above two million dollars a year.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill adding a 10% surtax on income above $2 million ($1 million for single filers) was referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2026 and has not received a committee vote; it has three Democratic cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a new 10 percent tax on top of existing income taxes for individuals whose adjusted gross income tops $2 million, or $1 million for single filers. It defines income to include investment income, though it still allows a deduction for investment interest expenses. It takes effect for tax years beginning after 2026 and applies to estates and trusts as well as individuals.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday taxpayers in the sense that the cost falls entirely on households earning well over $1 million, not on middle- or working-class filers. If the revenue were later used for public programs, that would be a further benefit, though the bill itself does not direct the money anywhere.

how_it_helps.text: The surtax applies only to modified adjusted gross income above $2 million for joint filers and above $1 million for everyone else, so no household under those thresholds pays anything under the bill.
The tax reaches investment income, not just wages, because it applies to adjusted gross income, which includes capital gains and dividends; the bill also applies the surtax to estates and trusts.

analysis.who_pays: Households, estates, and trusts with annual income above $2 million (or $1 million for single filers), who would owe 10 cents of every additional dollar above that line, on top of existing taxes.

drawbacks.text: The surtax taxes income, not wealth, so it does not touch unrealized gains; a household whose wealth grows through assets it does not sell owes nothing under the bill, which limits how much of the very richest it reaches.
The bill still lets taxpayers reduce the income the surtax is measured on with deductions for investment interest expenses, so heavily leveraged investors owe less than the headline rate suggests.
The bill raises revenue but does not direct it to any specific use, so what ordinary people actually get from it depends entirely on later decisions by Congress.

An income spike in a single year, such as from a business sale, would trigger the tax even if the taxpayer's income is normally far lower, because the surtax is based on the year's income with no averaging.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households under the thresholds the bill costs nothing and simply places a 10 percent charge on income above $1-2 million. Its honest limits are that it taxes income rather than wealth, leaves a leveraged-investor deduction intact, and sends no revenue anywhere in particular. It is a narrow tax increase on the top sliver of earners, not a broad fix.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on April 15, 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no markup, hearing, or vote since.

narrative.text: Senator Van Hollen introduced the bill on April 15, 2026, joined by Senators Merkley, Luján, and Gallego.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day, which is the only action it has received.
No further action, hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled or recorded since referral, and the Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has lost anything; the households earning over $1 million who would pay the surtax are better off only in the sense that the bill has not moved, and the outcome remains open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The bill has not moved either way yet

for.name: Chris Van Hollen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Millionaires Surtax Act and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

for.name: Jeff Merkley, Ben Ray Luján, Ruben Gallego
for.role: U.S. Senators (OR, NM, AZ), original cosponsors

sides.party_line_note: No vote has taken place and no opposition has been recorded; all three cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill sits in the Finance Committee without a scheduled action.

industries.industry: Households earning over $1 million a year
industries.note: The bill would tax 10 percent of every dollar of their income above $1-2 million, on top of existing taxes. Because the cost falls only on top earners, their interest in blocking it runs against ordinary filers, who pay nothing under the bill.

industries.industry: Leveraged investment funds and high-income investors using borrowed money
industries.note: The surtax reaches their capital gains and dividends, but the bill lets them subtract investment interest deductions when measuring the income taxed, softening the hit for those who borrow to invest. Ordinary filers below the thresholds are unaffected either way.

analysis.trajectory: A single-sponsor tax bill with three cosponsors sitting in the Senate Finance Committee is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote in this Congress. Tax legislation in the Senate typically moves only through the Finance Committee or budget reconciliation with leadership backing, and none is visible here; the most likely path is that the bill sits without further action until the Congress ends.
